title: SQL Server & T-SQL
description: Progress from first SQL queries to robust data models, replayable imports, transaction contracts, query-plan diagnosis and an assessed reconciliation pipeline.
prerequisites: No SQL knowledge required. Comfort with files, rows and columns is helpful.
Access to a local or training SQL Server instance and a query client is needed to execute exercises; reading and quizzes work without one.
outcomes: Explain table grain, types, keys and NULL.
Write joins, aggregates, CTEs and window calculations with checked results.
Use typed parameters, temporary staging and rollback-based practice.
Reason about isolation and execution plans without misleading shortcuts.
Build an order/payment reconciliation that preserves unmatched records.
Specify decimal/time and migration contracts, not only query syntax.
Diagnose parameter-sensitive workloads and reason about Query Store evidence.
Design optimistic updates, bounded deadlock retries and least-privilege access.
Deliver a three-stage assessed import/reconciliation project with explicit validation limits.

Download setup.sql from this path. Review its comments and connect only to your training instance. A login needs permission to create LearningNotebook if it does not exist; otherwise ask the training administrator to create it.
Run setup.sql in SSMS and keep that query window open. All #LN fixture tables are session-local. In another window run setup.sql again to create a separate fixture.
Examples assume the setup fixture is unchanged. Start a new query window and run setup.sql to reset without modifying another session.
Run snippets or solutions.sql in the same session. GO is a client batch separator. Do not paste GO into an application driver call.

Advanced practice uses advanced-lab.sql and advanced-solutions.sql in the same session after setup.sql. It has a different payment-event dataset from the foundation fixture.

Stage exit projects require explained evidence. Selected downloadable fixtures, two-session races and Query Store were executed on SQL Server 2025 Express; see engine-verification.md. Crash durability and optional extensions remain unverified.

lessons.title: 1. Connect to a database and read a result
lessons.takeaway: SQL Server stores the data; a query tool sends instructions to it.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A SQL Server instance is a running database engine. One instance can contain several databases. A database contains objects such as tables; a schema groups named objects inside it. A row records one thing at a defined level of detail, and columns describe its attributes. In this course, one order row represents one order, not one payment or one customer.

T-SQL is Microsoft’s SQL dialect. SELECT retrieves a result; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is a client, not the engine itself. Installing a query tool alone does not create a running server. Connect to an existing local or training SQL Server instance for these exercises; do not use a work production connection.

The browser displays examples and checks your quiz answers; it does not execute SQL. Read setup.sql, run it in SSMS on your training instance, and keep that query window open. It creates LearningNotebook only if absent and uses session-local #LN tables. Opening a second window creates a different session, so its temporary tables are separate.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: The first statement identifies the database and engine version so a result is attached to a real environment. The second counts our five sample orders. GO in the download is a client batch separator recognised by SSMS and sqlcmd; it is not a T-SQL statement to send through a database API.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Check the connection and database before a query that changes data. Our examples use fixed synthetic data; matching a row count is evidence about this fixture, not proof that a production extract is complete. Closing the session removes its local temporary tables. Reopen setup.sql to get a fresh fixture.

exercise.prompt: After running setup.sql, return each customer identifier and name, ordered by identifier.

exercise.solution: SELECT CustomerId, CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Four rows: 1 Ada, 2 Ben, 3 Chen, 4 Dia.
Column names are explicit; ordering is requested.

quiz.question: What makes the #LNOrders data available to your next query?
options: Running setup.sql in the same SQL session
quiz.explanation: Local temporary tables belong to a SQL session. Use the same connection/window after setup.

lessons.title: 2. Choose types, keys and missing-value rules
lessons.takeaway: A schema expresses what each value means and which rows are valid.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Use int for these identifiers, decimal(12,2) for the sample amounts, date for dates without a time, and nvarchar for Unicode names. Decimal has a fixed precision and scale; it is useful when two decimal places are part of the business contract. It does not solve every rounding decision. Avoid float for amounts that must compare exactly to a cent.

A primary key uniquely identifies a row and cannot contain NULL. A foreign key in an ordinary permanent table enforces a relationship to an existing parent key. A CHECK constraint restricts allowed values. A constraint prevents invalid writes; an application-side check alone can be bypassed by another writer. SQL Server does not enforce foreign keys on temporary tables, so our fixture uses explicit validation queries for relationships.

NULL means missing or unknown, not zero and not an empty string. Email is optional in the fixture: Ben and Dia have NULL. Equality with NULL does not produce TRUE, so use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Decide whether an unknown amount should stop a report rather than quietly substituting zero.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: COUNT(*) counts all four customers; COUNT(Email) counts the two known emails. The unassigned payment for OrderId 999 is intentionally allowed in the staging fixture. A production payment table with an enforced foreign key would reject it; an incoming staging table may retain it for investigation.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A nullable column is a modelling decision, not a convenient default for everything. Define which identifiers are required, whether negative amounts represent refunds, and which currency is being counted. All amounts here are synthetic units in one currency.

exercise.prompt: Find customers whose email is known. Return their names in identifier order.
exercise.starter: SELECT CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers WHERE /* missing-value test */ ORDER BY CustomerId;
exercise.solution: SELECT CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers WHERE Email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Ada and Chen, in that order.
The predicate uses IS NOT NULL, not <> NULL.

quiz.question: How many rows does WHERE Email = NULL return in this fixture?
quiz.explanation: The comparison is UNKNOWN, not TRUE. WHERE retains TRUE rows; use IS NULL to select the two missing emails.

lessons.title: 3. Filter, calculate and sort deliberately
lessons.takeaway: A query needs explicit predicates, units and ordering.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: SELECT chooses output columns; FROM identifies input rows; WHERE keeps rows meeting a condition. ORDER BY is the output ordering contract. Without it, a familiar-looking order is not guaranteed. TOP without an ORDER BY does not mean the earliest or largest rows.

Use AND for conditions that must both hold and OR for alternatives; parentheses make mixed expressions unambiguous. Date predicates are easier to reason about as a lower bound inclusive and an upper bound exclusive. This also works when a date column later becomes a timestamp.

A computed column alias is available to ORDER BY, but generally not to WHERE in the same query because of SQL’s logical binding order. Logical order explains name scope; it is not a diagram of the optimizer’s physical execution plan.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Our orders are dated January 1, 2 and 3 of 2026. Filtering before January 3 keeps 101, 102 and 103; adding Amount >= 80 keeps 101 and 103. The ISO unseparated date literal avoids ambiguous regional day/month interpretation.
sections.example:
SELECT OrderId, Amount, Amount * 0.10 AS TenPercent
FROM #LNOrders
WHERE OrderDate >= '20260101' AND OrderDate < '20260103'
  AND Amount >= 80
ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId;
-- 101:100.00,10.0000; 103:80.00,8.0000 (display scale can vary)

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: SELECT * is convenient during exploration but makes downstream consumers depend on every future column. Integer arithmetic also matters: 5/2 yields 2, whereas CAST(5 AS decimal(10,2))/2 produces a fractional result. State required rounding at the output boundary.

exercise.prompt: Return the two largest orders, using OrderId as the tie-breaker.
exercise.starter: SELECT TOP (2) OrderId, Amount FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY /* criteria */;
exercise.solution: SELECT TOP (2) OrderId, Amount FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId;
checks: Ordering makes TOP meaningful and deterministic for tied amounts.

quiz.question: Which query gives a dependable largest-order result?
options: TOP (1) with ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId
quiz.explanation: TOP chooses from the requested order; a unique tie-breaker makes ties predictable.

lessons.title: 4. Join without losing or multiplying records
lessons.takeaway: Before joining, say what one row means on each side.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A customer can have many orders. Joining CustomerId therefore produces one output row per matching order, not one per customer. An INNER JOIN keeps matches. A LEFT JOIN also keeps each left-side row with no match, filling the right-side columns with NULL.

An order can have several payments: order 101 has payments 60 and 40. Joining orders directly to payments repeats the order amount for each payment. Summing those repeated amounts would exaggerate sales. Diagnose a join by checking key uniqueness, match counts and unmatched populations before summing money.

A filter on a right-hand column in WHERE can remove the NULL-extended rows of a LEFT JOIN. Put a right-side eligibility condition in ON when the requirement is to preserve all left rows and attach only qualifying right rows. This is a semantic choice, not a performance trick.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Dia has no order. LEFT JOIN preserves her as one row with a NULL OrderId. Customers 1 and 2 each appear twice; customer 3 once; customer 4 once, so the output has six rows.
sections.example:
SELECT c.CustomerId, c.CustomerName, o.OrderId
FROM #LNCustomers AS c
LEFT JOIN #LNOrders AS o ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
ORDER BY c.CustomerId, o.OrderId;
-- 1/101,1/102,2/103,2/104,3/105,4/NULL

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: DISTINCT is not a repair for an unexplained join expansion. It can hide duplicate evidence or discard legitimate repeated values. If the desired grain is one row per order, aggregate payments to that grain before joining; the next lesson builds that stage.

exercise.prompt: Find customers with no orders. Use an anti-match and return identifier/name.
checks: Only 4/Dia.
A LEFT JOIN with WHERE o.OrderId IS NULL is also correct.

quiz.question: Order 101 has two payment rows. What happens to its 100 order amount in a direct join?
options: It appears on both joined rows
quiz.explanation: Joining attaches matching rows; it does not allocate the order amount across them. Summing it now double counts.

lessons.title: 5. Aggregate at a stated grain
lessons.takeaway: GROUP BY collapses rows; WHERE and HAVING filter different stages.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Grouping by CustomerId returns one row per customer represented in the orders. SUM adds amounts; COUNT(*) counts rows; AVG calculates a mean of non-NULL values. Aggregates generally ignore NULL values, while COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of column values. An absent group is different from a group whose known amounts sum to zero.

WHERE limits input rows before grouping. HAVING limits groups after aggregate values exist. To count a customer’s orders after a LEFT JOIN, COUNT(o.OrderId) counts the matched non-NULL identifiers; COUNT(*) would count the placeholder row for a customer with no order.

Always label the denominator: average order value is total amount divided by order count, not by customer count. A mean of customer means is not the overall order mean unless the weights happen to match.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Customer 1 has 150 across two orders; customer 2 has 200 across two; customer 3 has 40 across one. The totals reconcile to 390 and five orders. A HAVING threshold of 150 includes 1 and 2.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount, SUM(Amount) AS Total
FROM #LNOrders
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING SUM(Amount) >= 150
ORDER BY CustomerId;
-- 1,2,150.00; 2,2,200.00

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A report that excludes customers with no orders may be fine for sales totals but wrong for customer coverage. Start from the customer table when that population must be preserved, and make the no-order policy explicit.

exercise.prompt: Return all four customers with order counts, including zero for Dia.
checks: Counts sum to 5; customer population stays 4.

quiz.question: Which clause filters a grouped customer total greater than 100?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results. WHERE is for the rows supplied to the grouping operation.

lessons.title: 6. Use CTEs and subqueries to name intermediate ideas
lessons.takeaway: A named query step improves reasoning; it is not automatically a stored result.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A subquery is a query inside another statement. EXISTS asks whether at least one matching row exists without multiplying the outer row. A common table expression (CTE) names a result within the next statement, so a long transformation can be read in stages.

A CTE is scoped to that one following statement. It is not a permanent table or a guaranteed performance cache. Prefix WITH with a semicolon when a preceding statement might lack its terminator. Multiple CTEs in one WITH are separated by commas.
For this report, first reduce payments to one row per OrderId, then attach that total to the orders. This changes the grain before the join so a two-payment order no longer duplicates its amount.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Order 104 has no payment total and is NULL after the join. COALESCE turns that absence into zero only for this specific amount calculation; retain a separate missing-payment indicator when it matters to the workflow.
sections.example:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId, SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId, o.Amount, COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS PaidAmount
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
-- 101:100;102:50;103:70;104:0;105:45 paid

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: NOT IN against a list containing NULL can unexpectedly reject rows because of UNKNOWN comparisons. NOT EXISTS with an explicit equality is usually a clearer expression for unmatched keys. Never discard unknown keys before recording their exception count.

exercise.prompt: Use NOT EXISTS to find incoming payments with an unknown OrderId.
exercise.starter:
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (/* correlated order lookup */);
checks: 206,999,20.00 is the single orphan.
The unknown payment is reported, not silently joined away.

quiz.question: Can a CTE name be reused by an unrelated second SELECT statement?
options: No, its scope is the next statement
quiz.explanation: A CTE names a query expression for one statement. Use a temporary table when a later statement needs stored intermediate rows.

lessons.title: 7. Rank rows and compute running totals
lessons.takeaway: A window calculation retains detail rows while looking across related rows.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: GROUP BY collapses a group to fewer rows. A window function uses OVER to calculate across a related set while keeping each original row. PARTITION BY starts a separate window per customer; ORDER BY defines sequence within it.

ROW_NUMBER assigns sequential numbers. To select the latest order reliably, order by OrderDate descending and then OrderId descending. The identifier resolves same-date ties. RANK and DENSE_RANK treat ties differently, so select a function to match the business question rather than because its name sounds right.

For a running sum, explicitly use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That means every preceding row plus this one in the specified order. The outer query still needs ORDER BY to control display order.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Ben’s two orders occur on January 2 and 3, so his running total is 80 then 200. Ada’s is 100 then 150; Chen’s is 40. The result still has five order rows.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, OrderId, Amount,
 SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS RunningTotal
FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY CustomerId,OrderDate,OrderId;

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: ROW_NUMBER is not a stored primary key. It can change when the input changes. For latest-row selection, rank in a CTE and filter rn=1 outside it; the alias cannot be filtered in WHERE in that same SELECT.

exercise.prompt: Return the latest order for each customer who has orders.
exercise.starter:
;WITH Ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY /* latest */) AS rn FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT CustomerId,OrderId FROM Ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY CustomerId;
exercise.solution:
;WITH Ranked AS (SELECT CustomerId,OrderId,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC,OrderId DESC) AS rn FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT CustomerId,OrderId FROM Ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Dia is absent because she has no order; include her only through a separate population join.

quiz.question: Why add OrderId after OrderDate to the ranking order?
quiz.explanation: A unique tie-breaker prevents equal dates from leaving the selected latest row ambiguous.

lessons.title: 8. Use parameters and stored procedures
lessons.takeaway: Pass data as typed parameters; keep SQL text separate from values.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A parameter is a named input with a declared SQL type. Parameters make the value contract explicit and avoid building SQL by concatenating user text. Applications should bind parameters through their database driver. Parameterization helps prevent value-based SQL injection; it is not a replacement for access control or input validation.

A stored procedure is a named database program invoked with EXEC. It can contain queries and control flow. SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses row-count messages, not the query result. The lesson example creates a local temporary procedure, so it disappears when this SQL session ends and changes no permanent application code.

In SSMS, CREATE PROCEDURE belongs in its own batch. The GO separators below are important. The procedure relies on the caller’s temporary fixture only for this lesson; a deployed procedure normally uses explicitly qualified permanent tables with a designed permission model.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Requesting CustomerId 2 produces orders 103 and 104. Calling the same procedure for 4 gives an empty result because Dia has no orders. That is a legitimate result, not a SQL exception.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Identifiers such as table names cannot be supplied as ordinary value parameters. If identifiers must vary, use a controlled allowlist and appropriate quoting. Do not concatenate them from arbitrary input. Different parameter values can also have different selectivity: reusing a plan is not a guarantee of good performance.

exercise.prompt: Use sp_executesql with a typed parameter to return orders with amounts at least 90; do not concatenate 90 into the SQL text.
exercise.starter: EXEC sys.sp_executesql N'SELECT OrderId,Amount FROM #LNOrders WHERE Amount>=@Minimum ORDER BY OrderId;', /* type declaration */, /* value */;
exercise.solution: EXEC sys.sp_executesql N'SELECT OrderId,Amount FROM #LNOrders WHERE Amount>=@Minimum ORDER BY OrderId;', N'@Minimum decimal(12,2)', @Minimum=90;
checks: @Minimum is declared and supplied separately from statement text.

quiz.question: What should an application do with a user-supplied minimum amount?
options: Bind it as a typed parameter
quiz.explanation: Typed parameters separate values from executable SQL text. Validate business limits and use least-privilege permissions as well.

lessons.title: 9. Stage work and practise safe data changes
lessons.takeaway: Temporary tables store intermediate rows; changes still need a clear scope.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A # temporary table exists in tempdb with session-local visibility. Unlike a CTE, it can be reused by later statements and can have indexes. It consumes resources and is not automatically faster; choose it when inspecting, indexing or reusing an intermediate result helps.

INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, and DELETE removes matching rows. A missing WHERE on an UPDATE or DELETE affects every row. For practice, we change a dedicated #LNWork copy rather than the base fixture, and put the demonstration inside a transaction that rolls back.

SELECT INTO creates a new table from query output. It does not mean every constraint and index from the source has been reproduced. For a controlled production staging design, CREATE TABLE first and explicitly INSERT the selected columns.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: The script copies five orders, adds 10 to order 103, observes 90, then rolls back to 80. The copied table exists before BEGIN TRAN, so it remains after rollback. Rerunning this example replaces only the session-local work copy.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Record @@ROWCOUNT immediately after the relevant modification: subsequent statements can replace it. A targeted update that affects zero rows may indicate a missing identifier or concurrency conflict. Inspect it rather than claiming success because no exception occurred.

exercise.prompt: Copy orders to #LNExerciseWork and delete only order 105 inside a transaction. Show the row count before rollback; then prove all five rows remain.
exercise.starter: -- Create a temporary work copy, BEGIN TRAN, DELETE with WHERE, inspect @@ROWCOUNT, ROLLBACK.
checks: DeletedRows=1; RemainingRows=5.
The original #LNOrders still contains all five rows.

quiz.question: When should you capture @@ROWCOUNT after an UPDATE?
quiz.explanation: @@ROWCOUNT describes the previous relevant statement and can be reset by subsequent statements.

lessons.title: 10. Make a unit of work atomic and consider concurrency
lessons.takeaway: A transaction groups changes; isolation determines what concurrent sessions can observe.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: BEGIN TRAN starts an explicit transaction; COMMIT completes it; ROLLBACK undoes its transactional changes. Atomicity means the unit succeeds together or is undone. Keep transactions short and avoid waiting for a person while locks are held. A client disconnect or timeout is not a substitute for a designed error-handling strategy.

TRY/CATCH lets this example roll back when a statement fails. SET XACT_ABORT ON makes many runtime errors terminate and roll back the transaction. In CATCH, XACT_STATE reports whether a transaction remains and whether it is committable; THROW propagates the original error.

Isolation is about overlapping sessions. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, but a later statement can see newly committed changes. Its implementation depends on the database’s READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT setting. SNAPSHOT needs database configuration and gives a transaction-level versioned view; SERIALIZABLE protects ranges more strongly and can increase blocking. NOLOCK permits unreliable reads and is unsuitable as a reconciliation fix.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: This deliberately throws after an update to a work copy. The CATCH rolls it back and returns an explanatory result instead of rethrowing, solely so the final verification runs. A real application should usually propagate the failure. Starting an outer transaction beforehand would change rollback scope; run the exercise with @@TRANCOUNT=0.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Single-session temporary tables cannot demonstrate inter-session blocking because other sessions cannot access them. For a later concurrency lab, have a trainer supply a dedicated shared table and a two-session script. Do not change isolation database options on a shared database just to make an example run.

sections.title: Runnable opt-in engine experiment
paragraphs: The downloadable concurrency-lab.md gives a dedicated disposable database with explicit opt-in, two guarded session scripts, timed schedules, expected assertions and ownership-checked cleanup. Use separate A/B connections; existing session-local #LN tables cannot demonstrate a shared-row race. Record actual engine results rather than labeling the expected schedule as executed evidence.

The lab contrasts dirty/committed reads, demonstrates stale read-modify-write loss and an atomic increment remedy, and forces a low-priority deadlock victim with whole-transaction rollback. The Query Store script captures repeated identical query text before/after an index and returns persisted plans, runtime intervals and metrics; no particular speedup or plan shape is promised.

exercise.prompt: Inspect this database’s row-versioning settings without changing them. Explain why the result matters for READ COMMITTED.
exercise.starter: SELECT name, /* row versioning flags */ FROM sys.databases WHERE name=DB_NAME();
exercise.solution: SELECT name,is_read_committed_snapshot_on,snapshot_isolation_state_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name=DB_NAME();
checks: One row for LearningNotebook; exact flag values depend on setup and are not assumed.
Explain statement-level versioning when READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is enabled.

quiz.question: Does READ COMMITTED guarantee two SELECT statements see identical data?
options: No, another transaction may commit between them
quiz.explanation: Avoiding dirty reads is different from holding a stable view across multiple statements.

lessons.title: 11. Read a plan before tuning a query
lessons.takeaway: Indexes trade read access paths against storage and write costs.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An index is an additional access structure the optimizer may use. A clustered rowstore index organizes the table’s rows by its key; a nonclustered index provides another ordered access path with a row locator. An INCLUDE column can cover output without being part of the search key. More indexes also mean more maintenance during writes.

An execution plan shows chosen operators such as scans, seeks, sorts and joins. Estimated plans show predictions; actual plans add runtime information. Compare estimated and actual row counts, warnings and expensive work, not only the largest percentage label. A seek is not automatically good and a scan is not automatically bad.

A predicate such as OrderDate >= @From AND OrderDate < @To can support an index range access more naturally than wrapping OrderDate in YEAR(). Whether an index is chosen still depends on data volume, distribution, statistics and required output. Our five-row fixture is too small to establish performance gains.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Create an index on a temporary copy, enable statistics, and inspect the actual plan in SSMS. The returned values must stay unchanged. With five rows the optimizer may prefer a scan, and either elapsed time can round to zero: this is a plan-reading exercise.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Do not add every suggested missing index or force a join hint without a representative workload. A fast query that drops unmatched records is still wrong. First freeze the correctness checks, then compare evidence on data and parameters representative of actual use.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite YEAR(OrderDate)=2026 as a range predicate. Return only OrderId and verify all five identifiers.
exercise.starter: SELECT OrderId FROM #LNOrders WHERE /* half-open date range */ ORDER BY OrderId;
exercise.solution: SELECT OrderId FROM #LNOrders WHERE OrderDate>='20260101' AND OrderDate<'20270101' ORDER BY OrderId;
checks: No function is applied to OrderDate; no speed improvement is claimed from this tiny fixture.

quiz.question: What should you conclude if the five-row table still uses a scan after adding an index?
options: A scan may be the sensible plan at this size
quiz.explanation: Plan quality depends on the cost of the whole operation and the data; operator names alone do not establish performance.

lessons.title: 12. Build an order-to-payment reconciliation
lessons.takeaway: A trustworthy report preserves populations, reconciles totals and exposes exceptions.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Your stakeholder wants to know which orders are paid. Define the grain as one row per order, the scope as all five fixture orders, and the matching rule as OrderId. All amounts share one currency. Payment rows are staging observations: an unknown order is an exception to report, not evidence that an order should be invented.

First aggregate the six payment rows by OrderId. Then left join the five orders to that result. Keep missing payment evidence separate from a known total of zero, and calculate outstanding as amount due minus matched payments. A negative outstanding amount means overpayment in this teaching contract.

The report has two outputs: five order rows and an orphan-payment list. A grand-total subtraction of 390-285=105 is misleading for order balances because 20 of incoming payments belongs to unknown OrderId 999. Matched payments total 265, leaving net outstanding 125. Positive outstanding is 130; overpayment is 5; net 130-5=125.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Expected order statuses:101 paid,102 paid,103 underpaid by 10,104 missing with 120 outstanding,105 overpaid by 5. The orphan list contains 206/999/20. Check both row counts and values; a result containing the right total but duplicated rows is not acceptable.
sections.example:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId,COUNT(*) AS PaymentCount,SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount
 FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId,o.Amount AS Due,COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Paid,
 o.Amount-COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Outstanding,
 CASE WHEN p.OrderId IS NULL THEN 'missing'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount=o.Amount THEN 'paid'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount<o.Amount THEN 'underpaid'
      ELSE 'overpaid' END AS Status
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #LNOrders o WHERE o.OrderId=p.OrderId)
ORDER BY p.PaymentId;

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A rerun must not append duplicate logical exceptions. A real pipeline needs source batch identifiers, source-row keys, duplicate policy, currency, effective time and approval rules. This capstone produces read-only results, so repeated execution does not post transactions. Duplicated PaymentId rows would be rejected by the fixture primary key; duplicate business events with different identifiers still require a separate policy.

exercise.prompt: Write the two report outputs without looking at the solution. Explain why the orphan 20 is excluded from matched paid totals. Then describe how a duplicate payment event would change your design.

-- 2 LEFT JOIN to the order population.
-- 3 CASE classify missing/paid/underpaid/overpaid.
-- 4 NOT EXISTS for orphan payments.

 FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId,o.Amount AS Due,COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Paid,
 o.Amount-COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Outstanding,
 CASE WHEN p.OrderId IS NULL THEN 'missing'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount=o.Amount THEN 'paid'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount<o.Amount THEN 'underpaid'
      ELSE 'overpaid' END AS Status
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #LNOrders o WHERE o.OrderId=p.OrderId)

Due 390, matched paid 265, net outstanding 125.
Status counts:paid 2,underpaid 1,missing 1,overpaid 1.
All payment amounts 285 = matched 265 + orphan 20.
A duplicate-event policy is described without silently using DISTINCT on monetary values.

quiz.question: Why is 390 minus 285 not the correct net outstanding for known orders?
options: The 285 includes 20 assigned to an unknown order
All payment rows should be removed
quiz.explanation: Only 265 is matched to known orders. Preserve the remaining 20 as an orphan exception instead of using it to reduce known balances.

lessons.title: 13. Model constraints, decimal amounts and time
lessons.takeaway: A schema is a business contract; precision, identity and time are part of correctness.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: A surrogate key identifies a database row; a business key identifies the event or entity outside the database. A payment identity column does not stop the same source payment being imported twice. Keep a stable source-system/event key and enforce its uniqueness in a permanent target. Decide whether corrections replace an event or create a new revision before choosing that key.

Separate an order header from its lines: customer and order date belong to the order; product, quantity and unit price belong to a line. Storing a customer address repeatedly in order rows may be appropriate as a historical shipping snapshot, but inappropriate if meant to be a current customer lookup. Normalization and historical snapshots solve different requirements.

decimal(p,s) has p total digits and s fractional digits. Arithmetic can widen the intermediate precision and scale, with SQL Server rules and maximum precision limiting the result. Explicitly choose the posting scale and test overflow and half-cent cases. A CHECK on amount alone does not reject NULL; combine NOT NULL with the check when an amount is required.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: Three units at 12.35 total 37.05. The timestamp is a different problem: a local January 1 observation corresponds to December 31 in UTC. A date bucket therefore requires a stated reporting zone, not simply stripping the offset.

datetimeoffset preserves an offset, not a named time-zone rule set. Store an event’s observed instant and, when required, its source zone/offset and ingestion time separately. Daylight-saving conversion needs an explicit policy for ambiguous local times.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Keep a rate at sufficient precision until the prescribed rounding boundary; rounding each line and rounding an invoice total can differ. Test both and choose the business rule explicitly. Do not silently turn malformed input into zero.

Our temporary fixtures cannot enforce foreign keys. Describe the permanent foreign-key design, then validate parent references with queries in this lab. A migration to permanent tables needs a real constraint test in SQL Server before deployment.

sections.title: Visible decimal normalization
paragraphs: Run rounding-lab.sql: raw 1.004 becomes decimal(12,2) 1.00; raw 1.005 becomes 1.01. Both are accepted scale conversion under this loader policy, while malformed, blank and negative amounts are rejected. The loader result includes AmountText and ParsedAmount together. Strict source-scale rejection needs a separate policy.

exercise.prompt: Calculate three items priced at 0.335: compare rounding each item to two decimals before summing with rounding the total. Explain which rule a contract must specify.
exercise.starter:
DECLARE @Unit decimal(12,3)=0.335;
SELECT /* rounded line total */, /* rounded invoice total */;
checks: RoundedLines=1.02; RoundedInvoice=1.01.
Explain that decimal precision does not decide the contractual rounding boundary.

quiz.question: Does a primary-key identity column alone prevent duplicate imports of one external event?
options: Yes, every inserted row has a different identity
No, enforce the external business key as well
Only if the amount is decimal
quiz.explanation: Two insertions can receive different identity values while representing the same source event.

lessons.title: 14. Compare sets and use correlated APPLY
lessons.takeaway: Set comparison, existence and per-row selection express different questions.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: UNION ALL concatenates input rows and preserves duplicates; UNION removes duplicates across all selected columns. EXCEPT returns distinct left-side rows absent from the right; INTERSECT returns distinct shared rows. These compare selected values, not hidden record identity. Matching keys alone can miss changed amounts.

EXISTS is a good fit for “does this customer have any order?” because it does not expand the outer population. A scalar subquery must return at most one value per outer row; a many-row result raises an error. Do not hide uncertainty with an arbitrary TOP without deterministic ordering.

APPLY evaluates a right-side table expression in relation to each left row. CROSS APPLY retains rows with a right result; OUTER APPLY also preserves left rows without one. This is useful for a latest order per customer, but does not guarantee a particular physical execution strategy.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: OUTER APPLY returns four customer rows including Dia. Changing it to CROSS APPLY removes Dia. The OrderId tie-breaker makes the TOP selection deliberate.

Set comparison treats NULLs as equal for distinctness in these operators. That differs from ordinary equality predicates and matters when checking snapshots containing nullable columns. The comparable columns also need compatible types and intended collation.
sections.example:
SELECT c.CustomerId, recent.OrderId, recent.Amount
FROM #LNCustomers c
OUTER APPLY (
 SELECT TOP(1) o.OrderId,o.Amount FROM #LNOrders o
 WHERE o.CustomerId=c.CustomerId ORDER BY o.OrderDate DESC,o.OrderId DESC
) recent ORDER BY c.CustomerId;
--1/102/50,2/104/120,3/105/40,4/NULL/NULL

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: EXCEPT is excellent for finding differences, but it does not report how many duplicate copies existed. Validate uniqueness separately. Likewise, UNION can hide a replayed payment if the selected values happen to match; replay handling belongs to business keys, not accidental row equality.

exercise.prompt: Find known order identifiers that do not appear in the incoming payment identifiers using EXCEPT, then explain why reversing the operands finds a different exception.
checks: First result 104: an order with no payment.
Reverse result 999: payment evidence with no known order.
Neither result diagnoses duplicate payment events.

quiz.question: You need all customers, including those without a latest order. Which operator fits?
quiz.explanation: OUTER APPLY retains the outer customer even if its correlated query produces no row.

lessons.title: 15. Specify window frames and compare consecutive observations
lessons.takeaway: A moving window is defined by rows or values; it is not automatically a time interval.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: LAG accesses a preceding row in a specified order; LEAD accesses a following row. The first LAG result is NULL unless a default is supplied. Replacing this with zero changes the meaning from “no previous observation” to a numerical baseline, so choose deliberately.

ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means at most two rows, even if they are minutes or months apart. A seven-row mean is not a seven-day mean when dates are missing or several observations share a date. For calendar windows, define a calendar or explicit time-range join.

With an ORDER BY, an aggregate window’s implicit frame can include peers under RANGE semantics. Explicit ROWS plus a stable tie-breaker is the clearer running-row contract. Ranking ties, peer totals and running sequence are separate requirements.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The sample has five rows ordered by date then identifier. Its two-row sums are 100, 150, 130, 200 and 160. These are adjacent-order amounts across all customers; adding PARTITION BY CustomerId changes the question.

A gaps-and-islands problem first defines adjacency, such as consecutive calendar days or consecutive event sequence numbers. Deduplicate to the intended grain before labelling islands. Otherwise repeated dates can create misleading sequence differences.
sections.example:
SELECT OrderId,OrderDate,Amount,
 LAG(Amount) OVER(ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId) AS PreviousAmount,
 SUM(Amount) OVER(ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS TwoRows
FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId;
--TwoRows:100,150,130,200,160

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Window functions do not repair an ambiguous event order. If ingestion time differs from business time, include the chosen time and tie-breaker in the output so reviewers can reconstruct the sequence. Late arrivals may legitimately change historical running values.

exercise.prompt: For each customer’s orders, return previous order amount and difference from it. Preserve NULL for a first order.
exercise.starter:
;WITH Compared AS (SELECT CustomerId,OrderId,Amount, /* LAG */ AS PreviousAmount FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT *,Amount-PreviousAmount AS Change FROM Compared ORDER BY CustomerId,OrderId;
exercise.solution:
;WITH Compared AS (SELECT CustomerId,OrderId,Amount,LAG(Amount) OVER(PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId) AS PreviousAmount FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT CustomerId,OrderId,Amount,PreviousAmount,Amount-PreviousAmount AS Change FROM Compared ORDER BY CustomerId,OrderId;
checks: Customer 1:NULL then -50; customer 2:NULL then 40; customer 3:NULL.
Explain why the first difference stays NULL.

quiz.question: A seven-row window contains two records from one day and misses another day. Is it a seven-day metric?
options: No, row count and elapsed days differ
Yes, SQL always fills missing dates
Yes, when you sort by date
quiz.explanation: A row frame follows positions in the ordered rows; it does not synthesize a calendar.

lessons.title: 16. Design an index for a query and inspect estimates
lessons.takeaway: An index proposal needs a workload, a predicate contract and measured evidence.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: Sargability describes whether a predicate can support useful search arguments on an access structure. Avoid unnecessary functions or implicit conversions on indexed columns. Match parameter types to column types so the engine does not have to convert the column for comparison. This helps possibilities; it does not force an index seek.

For the query “one customer during a date range,” an index beginning with CustomerId then OrderDate is a candidate. Amount is output only, so it can be included. Reversing the key order may help other date-only queries instead. Index order is a workload trade-off, not a universal selectivity slogan.

Statistics help estimate cardinality, meaning how many rows flow through an operator. A histogram describes the leading statistics key and has limited steps; skew and correlation can still make estimates inaccurate. An index existing does not imply its estimates represent today’s data.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: This repeats the small index lab with explicit parameter types and a half-open date range. It is suitable for reading a plan, not proving speed. Record actual versus estimated rows and logical reads with the same parameters and fixture.

On a large representative training dataset, compare a common customer with a rare one. A plan that works well for one distribution may be expensive for the other. Capture query, parameters, indexes, statistics state and compatibility level before drawing a conclusion.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Every extra index costs space and write work. A covering index that adds many wide columns may be a poor trade. Update statistics or change an index only under a controlled experiment; repeatedly clearing a shared plan cache is not an acceptable benchmark method.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite the predicate YEAR(OrderDate)=@Year for a typed integer parameter, and propose an index for a customer-plus-year query. State what you would measure.

DECLARE @Year int=2026,@Customer int=2;
-- Use DATEFROMPARTS and DATEADD, then an inclusive/exclusive range.
checks: Orders 103 and 104.
State valid @Year bounds if input is external; DATEFROMPARTS rejects invalid years.
Do not claim a performance win on five rows.

quiz.question: A query estimates ten rows and reads a million. What is a useful next step?
options: Inspect statistics, predicates, parameters and data skew
quiz.explanation: Cardinality errors can come from several causes. Preserve the evidence before selecting a remedy.

lessons.title: 17. Give procedures explicit transaction and error contracts
lessons.takeaway: A reusable procedure must specify inputs, outputs, transaction ownership and failures.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: A procedure contract includes permitted input ranges, result columns, expected row counts and error semantics. “It returned no SQL exception” is insufficient if an update silently matched zero rows. Check @@ROWCOUNT immediately after the modification.

Choose whether a procedure owns the transaction or participates in its caller’s transaction. This lab explicitly owns it and rejects an outer transaction. SQL Server nested BEGIN TRAN statements do not provide independent inner transactions: an unqualified ROLLBACK can undo the outer work. A composable production design needs an intentional savepoint/transaction-state policy.

TRY/CATCH handles many execution errors, but not every failure at the same execution level. Compile errors and client disconnections need application handling too. In CATCH, inspect transaction state, roll back owned work as appropriate, and THROW so the caller does not mistake failure for success.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The temporary procedure changes only #LNProcedureWork. A valid call changes order 103 from 80 to 81. An unknown order raises 51102 and leaves the work copy unchanged. Invalid amounts fail before any transaction starts.

The sample does not write an audit record or return a version token. Those are additional contract requirements when a caller must prove which update succeeded. Rerun the setup of this snippet to recreate the work copy; permanent fixture tables are not changed.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Avoid catching every error and returning a success-shaped empty table. Preserve useful error context while not exposing credentials or sensitive values. A rollback may also roll back an audit table insert in the same transaction; decide how operational failure logs are captured outside that unit.

exercise.prompt: After the worked example, call the procedure with nonexistent order 999 inside TRY/CATCH. Prove the work copy still has five rows and totals 391 after the earlier successful 81 update.
checks: Run the worked example first.
Error 51102; five rows; total 391; @@TRANCOUNT is zero after failure.

quiz.question: Why does this procedure reject an outer transaction?
options: Because SQL never supports nested BEGIN TRAN
Because a SELECT needs no transaction
To make its transaction ownership and rollback scope explicit
quiz.explanation: Nested transaction counters are not independent rollback boundaries. This lab adopts the simplest explicit ownership contract.

lessons.title: 18. Make an incremental load replayable
lessons.takeaway: Idempotency means a repeated logical input does not create a second business effect.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: A watermark such as “latest ingestion timestamp” helps select work but does not identify an event. Events can arrive late, clocks can differ, and a retry can replay an earlier batch. Keep stable source/event identifiers and a defined revision policy.

Distinguish identical duplicates from conflicting reuse of the same identifier. Two copies of E1 with amount 10 are a replay; E1 with 10 and 11 is a conflict requiring investigation or an explicit correction event. Choosing MAX(amount) would invent a business decision.

A target unique key is a last line of defence. NOT EXISTS avoids known rows in this single-session demonstration, but two simultaneous sessions can both observe absence. A production loader needs transaction/isolation design and duplicate-conflict handling; merely adding WHERE NOT EXISTS is not a concurrency proof.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: Run this snippet twice without replacing #LNReplayTarget. The first inserts two events; the second inserts none; the total stays 30. If you change E1 to 11, this simple loader skips it without detecting the conflict, demonstrating an intentional limitation.
The advanced capstone adds explicit validation, conflict and replay checks. Keep source observations long enough to explain why a row was accepted, rejected, quarantined or already processed.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Do not update the watermark before committing the target changes. A crash between those operations can lose work; replay-safe commits and durable source identifiers are more robust than relying on perfect timing. A schema migration must preserve those identifiers too.

sections.title: Visible decimal normalization
paragraphs: Run rounding-lab.sql: raw 1.004 becomes decimal(12,2) 1.00; raw 1.005 becomes 1.01. Both are accepted scale conversion under this loader policy, while malformed, blank and negative amounts are rejected. The loader result includes AmountText and ParsedAmount together. Strict source-scale rejection needs a separate policy.

exercise.prompt: Extend the replay check to find an incoming E1=11 that disagrees with stored E1=10 without updating the target.
exercise.starter: --Run the worked example first, then join incoming business keys to the target and compare payloads.

SELECT s.EventId,t.Amount AS StoredAmount,s.Amount AS IncomingAmount
FROM (VALUES(N'E1',CAST(11 AS decimal(12,2)))) s(EventId,Amount)
JOIN #LNReplayTarget t ON t.EventId=s.EventId WHERE t.Amount<>s.Amount;
--E1,10.00,11.00
checks: One conflict row; stored total remains 30.
Explain how an authorized correction could use a revision or compensating event rather than silently overwriting.

quiz.question: Does NOT EXISTS by itself make a concurrent import race-free?
options: No; overlapping transactions can both observe absence
Yes; SELECT reserves every absent key
quiz.explanation: A concurrency-safe design also needs enforced uniqueness and a deliberate transaction/error policy.

lessons.title: 19. Investigate regressions with plans and Query Store
lessons.takeaway: Compare like-for-like workload evidence before deciding that a plan change caused a slowdown.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: An actual plan reports operator runtime observations for an execution; Query Store retains historical query/plan/runtime information when enabled and capturing the workload. These answer different time scales. Availability, permissions and settings depend on the server version and database; do not assume the feature is enabled.

Start with a symptom: which query, time interval, parameters, row counts and workload changed? CPU, duration, logical reads, waits and execution count describe different costs. A rise in total duration might be more executions rather than slower individual calls.

Query Store runtime statistics are aggregated by intervals and execution types. If combining records, weight averages by execution count rather than averaging averages. Active intervals can have multiple entries for a plan; use the documented aggregation grain.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The diagnostic queries read options and known plans. An empty plan result can reflect capture settings, a new database or lack of applicable workload; it does not prove there were no queries. Do not enable or reconfigure Query Store on a shared system for this lesson.

Synthetic incident: planA averages 5 ms for 100 executions and planB averages 50 ms for 2. Combined mean is(500+100)/102, about 5.882 ms, not 27.5 ms. This arithmetic lesson is independent of whether your training database has captured plans.
sections.example:
--Read-only diagnostics in the selected training database; permission may be required.
SELECT DB_NAME() AS DatabaseName,actual_state_desc,desired_state_desc,
 current_storage_size_mb,max_storage_size_mb
FROM sys.database_query_store_options;
SELECT TOP(10) q.query_id,p.plan_id,p.is_forced_plan,qt.query_sql_text
FROM sys.query_store_query q
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON qt.query_text_id=q.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON p.query_id=q.query_id
ORDER BY q.query_id DESC,p.plan_id DESC;
--State, row count and contents depend on the instance; no fixed result is promised.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Plan forcing can be an operational mitigation, not proof of a permanent fix. Record why a prior plan is appropriate, its failure modes, how to unforce it, and what metric will trigger rollback. Parameter skew, statistics changes and blocking may require different remedies. This course does not force any plan.

paragraphs: The downloadable concurrency-lab.md gives a dedicated disposable database with explicit opt-in, two guarded session scripts, timed schedules, expected assertions and ownership-checked cleanup. Use separate A/B connections; existing session-local #LN tables cannot demonstrate a shared-row race. Record actual engine results rather than labeling the expected schedule as executed evidence.

The lab contrasts dirty/committed reads, demonstrates stale read-modify-write loss and an atomic increment remedy, and forces a low-priority deadlock victim with whole-transaction rollback. The Query Store script captures repeated identical query text before/after an index and returns persisted plans, runtime intervals and metrics; no particular speedup or plan shape is promised.

sections.title: Match the measured workload reliably
paragraphs: The downloadable lab identifies its dedicated procedure by object_id in Query Store. Exact text matching can miss automatically parameterized statements, while an inspection query can accidentally match its own text. Require captured successful runtime executions for the workload, not merely a matching query-text row. See engine-verification.md for the reproduced defect and negative control.

options: Only if Query Store is enabled

lessons.title: 20. Detect stale writes and reason about isolation
lessons.takeaway: Reading a value and later writing a replacement creates a concurrency contract.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: Imagine two users read amount 100. One saves 110; the other saves 120 based on the earlier 100. Blind last-writer-wins may erase the first decision. Decide whether overwriting is allowed, whether updates are additive, or whether stale writes must be rejected.

Optimistic concurrency checks a version captured with the original read. This lab uses an integer Revision column; production SQL Server often uses rowversion, which is a database-generated binary version token, not a date or wall-clock timestamp. The update includes both key and expected version; zero affected rows signals missing or changed data.

Pessimistic locking can instead protect the read-modify-write unit, with blocking and deadlock trade-offs. Snapshot reads reduce some reader/writer interference but do not remove the need to decide conflicting write behavior. Avoid presenting any isolation setting as a universal race fix.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The sequential script simulates two requests holding revision 1. The first succeeds and advances to 2; the second affects zero rows. This validates the predicate’s intention but is not a live two-session test.

In a real concurrency test, coordinate two sessions on a dedicated shared fixture, record start/commit ordering and expected results, and test retry/cancel paths. Our session-local tables intentionally cannot demonstrate cross-session contention.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: A version conflict is not an instruction to retry the same business decision blindly. Reload the current record and either merge, ask the user or reject according to policy. If a network error makes commit outcome uncertain, look up an operation identifier before repeating a non-idempotent effect.

sections.title: Runnable opt-in engine experiment
paragraphs: The downloadable concurrency-lab.md gives a dedicated disposable database with explicit opt-in, two guarded session scripts, timed schedules, expected assertions and ownership-checked cleanup. Use separate A/B connections; existing session-local #LN tables cannot demonstrate a shared-row race. Record actual engine results rather than labeling the expected schedule as executed evidence.

The lab contrasts dirty/committed reads, demonstrates stale read-modify-write loss and an atomic increment remedy, and forces a low-priority deadlock victim with whole-transaction rollback. The Query Store script captures repeated identical query text before/after an index and returns persisted plans, runtime intervals and metrics; no particular speedup or plan shape is promised.

options: The local time of the update
quiz.explanation: It supports detecting changes, but is not a datetime and does not replace a business event key.

lessons.title: 21. Diagnose deadlocks and bound retries
lessons.takeaway: A deadlock is a wait cycle; recovery needs both database and application reasoning.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: Blocking means one operation waits for another; a deadlock is a cycle in which participants cannot progress. SQL Server selects a victim and rolls back its transaction; error 1205 identifies a deadlock victim. A command timeout is a different event and can have a different transaction outcome.

Use the deadlock graph to identify resources, owners, waiters, statements and transaction boundaries. Do not assume the shortest displayed statement caused the whole problem. Access paths, lock escalation, isolation and triggers can affect the locks acquired.

A common mitigation is consistent access order and shorter transactions, plus appropriate access paths. It is a risk reduction, not an absolute guarantee. Retrying should be bounded, include backoff/jitter and repeat the complete safe unit after rollback, not only the last statement of a multi-step operation.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The two-session schedule shows a simple cycle. It is deliberately written as a reasoning artifact instead of a script that could leave sessions waiting. Draw the dependency edges and propose a consistent access order.

If the operation also sends an email or calls a payment API, database rollback cannot undo that external side effect. Use a durable outbox or another explicit delivery/idempotency contract; a generic retry loop around all application code can duplicate effects.
sections.example:
--Reasoning exercise, NOT executable SQL and not an induced deadlock.
Session A: BEGIN; lock order101; request order102.
Session B: BEGIN; lock order102; request order101.
A waits for B; B waits for A -> cycle.
Candidate change: both sessions access101 then102 in a short transaction.
Still test actual plans/lock resources: consistent logical ordering reduces risk,
but does not prove all deadlocks impossible.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: Collect evidence before adding hints. Lowering isolation can change correctness and may not resolve writer conflicts. Distinguish a known rolled-back deadlock victim from an unknown outcome after connection loss; the latter needs operation-status reconciliation.

sections.title: Runnable opt-in engine experiment
paragraphs: The downloadable concurrency-lab.md gives a dedicated disposable database with explicit opt-in, two guarded session scripts, timed schedules, expected assertions and ownership-checked cleanup. Use separate A/B connections; existing session-local #LN tables cannot demonstrate a shared-row race. Record actual engine results rather than labeling the expected schedule as executed evidence.

The lab contrasts dirty/committed reads, demonstrates stale read-modify-write loss and an atomic increment remedy, and forces a low-priority deadlock victim with whole-transaction rollback. The Query Store script captures repeated identical query text before/after an index and returns persisted plans, runtime intervals and metrics; no particular speedup or plan shape is promised.

exercise.prompt: Write retry pseudocode for an idempotent payment import with at most three attempts. Handle 1205 separately from validation errors and unknown commit outcomes.
exercise.solution: For each of at most3 attempts, open a clean transaction and execute the whole import using a stable operation/event key. On1205, verify transaction cleanup, wait with bounded jitter, then retry; on the third failure report exhaustion. On validation errors, fail immediately. On connection loss near commit, query durable operation status before retrying. Send external effects through an idempotent outbox after the transaction.
checks: Bounded three attempts, whole-unit retry, cleanup and backoff.
Validation failures are not retried.
Unknown commit outcomes are reconciled by stable operation key.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a deadlock from ordinary blocking?
options: A dependency cycle prevents the participants from progressing
Any slow SELECT is a deadlock
quiz.explanation: A wait can resolve when another transaction finishes. A cycle requires a participant to be broken out of it.

lessons.title: 22. Separate query values, identifiers and permissions
lessons.takeaway: Parameterization prevents one class of injection; authorization limits what a caller may do.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: Use parameters for values such as customer identifiers and amounts. A parameter cannot stand in for a table name or ORDER BY column identifier. If dynamic structure is required, select it from a fixed allowlist and quote the identifier; keep values parameterized.

A login authenticates at server scope and a database user represents access in a database, subject to the platform’s authentication model. Roles group permissions. Grant the narrow operations the application requires, such as execution of a vetted procedure, instead of db_owner or sysadmin for convenience.

Execution through a procedure can involve ownership chaining or other execution-context rules. Dynamic SQL can behave differently from static statements in that permission model. Test with the intended low-privilege identity, not only an administrator account.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The example allows only Amount or OrderId as a sort column and passes @Minimum independently. QUOTENAME handles identifier quoting, but it does not decide whether a caller should be allowed to request an identifier: that is the allowlist’s purpose.

The exercise changes no users or grants. For a real training permissions lab, have an administrator provision a dedicated user/role and test allowed/denied actions against a disposable schema. Do not create a powerful account as a shortcut.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: SQL text and parameter values in diagnostics may contain sensitive business data. Use synthetic data here and define who can read query history. Passwords and connection tokens belong in an appropriate secret store, not inside a stored procedure, browser path or committed script.

lessons.title: 23. Evolve a schema without breaking the running application
lessons.takeaway: A migration is a data and compatibility change with evidence and a recovery plan.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: An expand-and-contract migration first adds compatible structure, deploys writers/readers that understand it, backfills existing rows, validates them, and only later removes obsolete structure. Renaming or dropping a column while older application instances still use it can break a rolling deployment.

A migration history needs stable identifiers and a record of what was applied. An existence check alone is insufficient: a column may exist with the wrong type, nullability or meaning. Check expected preconditions and fail visibly when the actual schema diverges.

Backfilling currency illustrates the danger of a convenient default. In this synthetic fixture we stipulate USD; real records require authoritative currency evidence. For a large table, plan bounded batches, log growth, locks and application compatibility instead of assuming one giant UPDATE is harmless.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: The lab changes only a temporary copy. It adds a nullable column, fills it under the fixture contract, verifies no NULL remains, then tightens nullability. Count and amount stay 5 and 390.

This is a shape-of-migration demonstration, not a production deployment script. Index rebuilds and schema modifications may require stronger locks and version-specific capabilities; verify on a representative training environment.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: A down migration cannot always restore lost data or reverse a business transformation. Define recovery in terms of backups, compatible app rollback and forward repair. Keep historical migration files immutable after release; add a corrective migration rather than rewriting applied history.

exercise.prompt: Write preflight and postflight checks for introducing CurrencyCode. Explain what must happen before a real legacy column is removed.
exercise.starter: --State compatibility, data-source, nullability, row-count and amount reconciliation checks.
exercise.solution: Preflight: verify schema version, supported app versions, authoritative currency mapping and a recoverable backup/restore plan. Expand nullable CurrencyCode; deploy compatible code; backfill in monitored batches. Postflight: zero invalid/null codes, per-currency totals reconciled, unchanged business-key population, old and new reads equivalent for supported requests. Remove a legacy column only after all readers/writers have migrated and the rollback window has been considered.
checks: No invented default currency for real records.
Both schema shape and business totals are checked.
Removal waits for application compatibility evidence.

quiz.question: A column already exists. Is that sufficient proof that a migration has been correctly applied?
options: No, inspect type, nullability, semantics and migration history
quiz.explanation: An existence check cannot detect an incompatible or partially applied schema change.

lessons.title: 24. Deliver an auditable, replayable import and reconciliation
lessons.takeaway: A production-shaped pipeline accounts for every input and proves its replay behavior.

sections.title: Model the problem
paragraphs: Download advanced-lab.sql and advanced-solutions.sql. Run the foundation setup first, then the advanced fixture in the same SQL session. This second fixture is intentionally different from the foundation payments: six raw rows include an exact duplicate, an orphan and an invalid amount. Do not compare its 215 accepted amount with the earlier 265 matched total as if they were the same dataset.

Keep raw rows immutable for the run. Parse types while retaining original text, identify conflicting payloads per business key, distinguish duplicate copies, then classify invalid and orphan records before loading accepted events. A rejected row must remain traceable to its RawRowId and reason.

The downloadable solution uses a conservative payload conflict rule: different amount strings under the same event key are conflicts, even when they might parse to equal amounts. It permits decimal scale conversion during parsing. Those are explicit teaching policies, not universal financial-import rules. A stricter input format/scale rule should be added if the source contract requires it.

sections.title: Work the example
paragraphs: First pass: accepted 3, duplicate 1, orphan 1, invalid 1. The ledger receives E001=100, E002=70 and E003=45, totalling 215. Replay inserts zero and retains the same total. The report preserves all five orders; net outstanding is 175.

Add a contradictory E002=75 as a separate raw row only in a disposable copy/session. Both E002 observations are classified as conflict, not resolved by picking the largest amount. If the original 70 was already loaded, quarantine does not retract it automatically: an authorized correction/reversal policy must reconcile the ledger and new evidence.

sections.title: Trade-offs and failure cases
paragraphs: The exercise demonstrates logical replay handling in one session. A real loader must add durable batches, enforced keys, concurrent-writer tests, transaction retry behavior, access controls and monitoring. Local temporary tables cannot establish durable crash recovery or cross-session locking correctness.

Submit evidence, not only a final query: disposition counts, ledger keys and totals, before/after replay checks, proposed concurrency policy, migration plan and least-privilege boundary. Mark tests requiring a real engine as unexecuted until you actually run them.

project.title: Order-to-payment control report
project.brief: Use the original setup.sql dataset to produce a customer/order report and a separate orphan-payment result.
requirements: Preserve all five orders and report Dia as a customer with no order.
Aggregate payment rows before joining; classify missing,paid,underpaid and overpaid.
Reconcile incoming payments and known-order totals; include deterministic ordering.
rubric: Reasoning:explain why direct payment joins can duplicate order values.
Evidence:show queries, outputs and at least one deliberately wrong query corrected.
project.solution:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId,COUNT(*) AS PaymentCount,SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount
 FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId,o.Amount AS Due,COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Paid,
 o.Amount-COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Outstanding,
 CASE WHEN p.OrderId IS NULL THEN 'missing'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount=o.Amount THEN 'paid'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount<o.Amount THEN 'underpaid'
      ELSE 'overpaid' END AS Status
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #LNOrders o WHERE o.OrderId=p.OrderId)
ORDER BY p.PaymentId;
--Customer coverage: select all customers and use NOT EXISTS to identify Dia.
--Accepted evidence:due390=paid265+net125;payments285=matched265+orphan20.
